script.opening: (Support worker Maria speaks; Danny sits beside her, anxious, looking at her rather than the screen.) "Thanks for seeing us, doctor. Danny's support team asked me to bring him — he's been having blood when he goes to the toilet, for a couple of months now, and his poos have been looser and more often — his pads have been soiled more. He's gone off his food and I think he's lost a bit of weight. He gets very anxious about appointments, so I hope it's okay that I'm here to help. Danny, it's alright — the doctor's kind."

facts.text: Danny (played by the role-player) answers in short phrases if asked simply and directly, and looks to Maria for help. Says yes to things he doesn't understand unless the doctor checks. Likes being called Danny. Loves football (Arsenal) — relaxes if this is mentioned.
(Danny) "Red. In the toilet." (Maria) "Sometimes it's on the paper, sometimes it's mixed in." About two months. No black stools seen.
(Danny shrugs) "Don't know." (Maria) "He hasn't told us about any pain." If the doctor asks Danny to point on camera where it hurts, he points vaguely at his lower tummy, then shrugs.

(Maria) "About two months. Looser, and more often" — four or five times a day, used to be once. "He's gone off his food, and I think he's lost a bit of weight, but we haven't weighed him properly." His jeans are looser. (Maria) "It's definitely new. Honestly, I was worried someone would say it's just his nerves."
(Maria) "No, nothing like that" — no vomiting, no fevers, no new behaviour change, no breathlessness. A bit more tired and sleeping more in the afternoons.

Down's syndrome, moderate learning disability. Hypothyroidism? — (Maria) "I don't think so — he's not on any tablets." Annual health check last done 18 months ago. No allergies. No family history known (lived in care since his mum died).
Lives in supported living with 24-hour staff. Maria has supported him for 6 years. His sister, Grace, is his next of kin and visits monthly. No lasting power of attorney.

(Maria) "He finds blood tests really hard." If the doctor explains the stool test and blood test simply and asks Danny: (Danny) "Scared." If reassured that Maria can come: (Danny nods) "Maria come." He can repeat back "Blood. In poo." when asked why.

Danny is anxious but responds to warmth, being spoken to directly and simple words. If the doctor only talks to Maria, Danny looks away and stops answering. Maria is helpful and protective; becomes visibly relieved if the doctor rules out "it's just his nerves": "Thank you. That's the first time someone's said they'll chase it."

ice.ideas: (Maria) The bleeding, looser stools and weight loss are new and need checking. (Danny) He doesn't know what is wrong, only that the toilet has blood in it.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA (Maria) — that Danny's symptoms will be put down to "his nerves" or his Down's syndrome, and that hospital tests will be too frightening for him so they never happen. (Danny) "Scared" of tests and of Maria not being there.
ice.expectations: A plan that actually gets Danny checked, with adjustments so he can cope — and someone to chase it.

cues: (Maria) "I was worried someone would say it's just his nerves." — the overshadowing fear.
(Danny) "Scared." — needs his own worries explored, not only Maria's.
(Maria) "He finds blood tests really hard." — invites reasonable adjustments.

checkpoints.text: Conducts an ADJUSTED CONSULTATION — communicates directly with Danny in accessible language at his pace, uses the support worker to facilitate not replace his voice, and offers reasonable adjustments (time, quiet space, easy-read, familiar person)

Actively AVOIDS DIAGNOSTIC OVERSHADOWING — takes rectal bleeding, bowel-habit change and weight loss as physical symptoms warranting full assessment, not attributing them to the learning disability/anxiety

Assesses CAPACITY per the Mental Capacity Act for the specific decisions (examination, FIT, referral) — presuming capacity, supporting it, and using best-interests with consultation if a specific decision-making capacity is lacking, documenting the process

Applies NICE NG12 and HTG690 (FIT-first): OFFERS FIT because he has a change in bowel habit (any age) and, at 50+, unexplained rectal bleeding and weight loss (IDA and an abdominal mass are also FIT indications) — FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway referral; knows only a rectal/anal mass or anal ulceration bypasses FIT — with a face-to-face examination (abdomen ± DRE if consented/tolerated) and FBC/ferritin, TFTs and coeliac serology

Makes the referral ACCESSIBLE — flags reasonable adjustments to the hospital (hospital passport, longer slots, support for bowel prep/procedure, anxiety planning) and sets up proactive tracking so investigation actually happens
Builds trust with an anxious patient — warm, unhurried, at Danny’s level — and works respectfully in the triad with the support worker without talking over Danny
Explains the plan in terms Danny and Maria can understand, checks understanding, and is honest about the seriousness without frightening

Safety-nets and follows up: clear plan for FIT/bloods/referral with adjustments, what to watch for, who to contact, ensures the appointment is navigable and actively tracked, documents capacity and adjustments, and arranges review — health-equity in the logistics, not a referral that is set up to fail

worked.txt: (Turning to Danny, gently, slowly.) "Hello Danny. I’m really glad you came in today. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions, and Maria can help if you want? … You’ve had some blood when you go to the toilet. That sounds worrying. Thank you for telling me — you did the right thing coming."

(To both.) "I want to be clear — bleeding, looser bowels and going off your food are things I take seriously in anyone, and Danny is no different. I’m not going to put this down to nerves; we need to find out what’s causing it."

"Danny, I’d like you to come to the surgery so I can feel your tummy — I can’t do that on the video — and we can do a simple poo test at home. I’ll explain each bit, and you can say stop any time. Is that okay with you? … Maria, you know Danny well — help me check he’s understanding, and we’ll go at his pace."

worked.lbl: Name the NICE NG12 plan plainly
worked.txt: "Here’s my plan. A poo test that looks for hidden blood, and a blood test — including his thyroid and a test for coeliac disease. Because of the bleeding, the change and the weight, if the poo test shows blood I’ll refer Danny to the bowel specialists on the urgent cancer pathway, where the aim is to have an answer within four weeks, usually with a camera test. And if I feel anything worrying when I examine him, I won’t wait for the poo test."

"I’ll tell the hospital that Danny needs a bit more time, a familiar face with him, and easy-read information — and I’ll note his hospital passport. Maria, let’s think now about how we make the camera test manageable for him — preparation, support on the day, maybe some sedation."

"If there’s a lot of blood, bad tummy pain, or Danny seems unwell, contact us straight away or go to A&E. I’m going to keep an eye on this myself to make sure the appointment comes through and nobody falls through the gap. We’ll see you back to go over the results together."

f.learning: This is the ADJUSTED CONSULTATION done well. Communicate directly WITH the patient — here Danny, who has Down’s syndrome and a learning disability — in short plain language at his pace, using the support worker to facilitate rather than replace his voice, and providing reasonable adjustments (longer appointment, quiet space, easy-read information, a familiar person), which are a legal duty under the Equality Act. The cardinal error to avoid is DIAGNOSTIC OVERSHADOWING: attributing new physical symptoms to the learning disability or to anxiety/behaviour. Rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit and weight loss are physical symptoms to be taken exactly as seriously as in anyone — arguably more so, given the stark health inequalities and premature mortality faced by people with learning disabilities. His symptoms meet the FIT criteria of NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) and NICE HTG690, which make colorectal referral FIT-first: FIT for a change in bowel habit at any age, and at 50+ for unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss (IDA and an abdominal mass are FIT indications too); FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway referral (the NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims to confirm or rule out cancer within 28 days of referral); only a rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration is referred without FIT. Examine face to face — not by video — (abdomen ± DRE if consented and tolerated), and check FBC/ferritin, TFTs and coeliac serology (NICE NG20; thyroid and coeliac disease are both commoner in Down’s syndrome). Assess CAPACITY for each specific decision under the Mental Capacity Act — presume it, support it, and only if a specific decision-making capacity is lacking act in best interests with consultation, documenting the process; capacity is decision-specific and never assumed absent because of the disability. Crucially, make the investigation ACCESSIBLE — flag reasonable adjustments and a hospital passport, plan for bowel prep/procedure and anxiety, and actively track the referral — because health inequality lives in the logistics, and a referral the patient cannot navigate is not care.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Code of Practice · Equality Act 2010 · NHS England Accessible Information Standard (DCB1605)
knowledge.summary: Rectal bleeding, looser stools and weight loss at 52 are a suspected colorectal cancer picture in anyone. Offer FIT, examine face to face, and refer on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more — with the reasonable adjustments that let Danny actually get through it.

points.t: NICE HTG690 and NICE NG12: offer quantitative FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. Danny qualifies on more than one count. FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer.

points.h: When not to wait for FIT
points.t: A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred on the examination finding without FIT. If FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g but strong clinical concern persists, NICE HTG690 says do not let the result delay referral.

Face-to-face abdominal examination and a DRE only with consent and at his pace. FBC and ferritin (iron-deficiency anaemia is itself a FIT indication), U&E, CRP, TFTs and coeliac serology (NICE NG20: offer testing for unexplained weight loss or persistent GI symptoms).

Do not put new physical symptoms down to the learning disability, Down’s syndrome or anxiety. LeDeR (Learning from lives and deaths) reviews repeatedly find delayed diagnosis of treatable illness in people with a learning disability.

Presume capacity; take all practicable steps to support it; assess for each decision (examination, FIT, colonoscopy) whether he can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate. If he lacks capacity for a specific decision, decide in his best interests after consulting those who know him, and record how you reached it.

Equality Act 2010 duty: longer or first-of-day appointments, a quiet space, easy-read information, a familiar supporter, and flagging adjustments on the referral (Accessible Information Standard; Reasonable Adjustment flag where available). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims to confirm or rule out cancer within 28 days of referral.

dg.d: Greeted Danny first; asked him directly, with pointing or showing as options; let Maria add, not replace.
Explored his usual toileting, eating and supported-living routine, the support team’s view, and the barrier of his anxiety about appointments.
Face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE with consent at his pace; FIT; FBC, ferritin, U&E, CRP, TFTs, coeliac serology.
Colorectal cancer, polyps, IBD, haemorrhoids or fissure, coeliac disease and thyroid disease — each tested, none assumed from the disability.
Screened for heavy bleeding, melaena, collapse; knows a rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration is referred without waiting for FIT.
Named a suspected colorectal cancer picture needing FIT and urgent investigation, stated without alarm.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Planned for anxiety about appointments and tests (numbing cream, familiar supporter, liaison nurse); flagged bowel prep support.

ro.d: Picked up Maria’s worry that it would be ‘put down to nerves’ and that the tests would be too much for him, and planned around both.

Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.

model.text: Hello Danny, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for coming on the video today. And hello Maria. Danny, is it okay if I talk to you, and Maria helps us if we need her?
model.why: Greets Danny first and asks his permission for the triad

model.text: (Danny looks at Maria, then nods.) “Okay.”

Thank you. Maria, I heard what you said about the blood and the looser stools. Danny, I’d like to understand what’s been happening, then decide together what we do next. We can go slowly, and you can say stop any time. Is that alright?
model.why: Sets a simple agenda and gives Danny control

model.text: (Maria) “That’s lovely, thank you. Danny, the doctor wants to hear from you.”
Danny, when you go to the toilet, do you see blood? You can point or show me, if that’s easier.
model.why: Short, concrete question to Danny, with a non-verbal option

model.text: (Danny) “Red. In the toilet.” (Maria) “Sometimes it’s on the paper, sometimes it’s mixed in.”
Thank you, Danny, that really helps. Does your tummy hurt? Can you show me where?
model.why: Asks about pain directly rather than through the carer

model.text: (Danny shrugs.) “Don’t know.” (Maria) “He hasn’t told us about any pain.”
Maria, you know Danny well. How has his toileting changed, and when did you first notice? And has he lost weight on the scales, or is it clothes fitting differently?
model.why: Uses the carer for collateral history on timing and weight

model.text: (Maria) “About two months. Looser, and more often. He’s gone off his food, and I think he’s lost a bit of weight, but we haven’t weighed him properly.”
That’s important. Is this different from how Danny usually is? I want to be sure we treat it as something new, not just ‘how he is’.
model.why: Establishes a baseline — the active guard against diagnostic overshadowing

model.text: (Maria) “It’s definitely new. Honestly, I was worried someone would say it’s just his nerves.”
Any vomiting, very dark or black stools, feeling faint, or bleeding a lot at once?
model.why: Screens for acute bleeding needing same-day care

model.text: (Maria) “No, nothing like that.”
Maria, you said you worried it might be put down to nerves. Can you tell me more about that?
model.why: Picks up the carer’s cue about being dismissed

model.text: (Maria) “Danny gets very anxious about appointments. I’m worried the hospital tests will be too much for him, and then they just won’t happen.”
Thank you — that’s exactly what I need to plan for. Danny, how do you feel about doctors and hospitals?
model.why: Brings Danny’s own feelings into the consultation

model.text: (Danny) “Scared.”
That makes sense, Danny. Lots of people feel scared of doctors. We’ll make a plan so it’s less scary, and Maria can be with you. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates the fear in plain words and offers support

model.text: (Danny nods.) “Maria come.”

Maria, let me be clear: blood from the bottom, looser stools and losing weight are things I take seriously in anyone of Danny’s age. His Down’s syndrome doesn’t change that — if anything, I want to be more careful, not less.
model.why: States plainly that the symptoms are physical and warrant full assessment

model.text: Danny, I’d like three things. One: a poo test you do at home — it looks for tiny bits of blood. Two: a blood test. Three: a check of your tummy, in person, with Maria there. Can you tell me back what the poo test is for?
model.why: Explains FIT, bloods and examination simply, then checks understanding

model.text: (Danny) “Blood. In poo.”

Exactly right. Well done. Maria, the test result decides how fast the hospital sees him, and I’m expecting to refer him urgently to the bowel team for a camera test. The aim is to know within about four weeks. I’ll put on the referral that he needs a longer slot, a familiar person with him, easy-read letters, and help with the bowel preparation. Does he have a hospital passport? If not, the team could put one together.
model.why: NICE NG12 FIT-led referral, with reasonable adjustments written into the referral

model.text: (Maria) “I’ll check with the team. What about his blood test — he finds that sort of thing really hard.”

I’ll book a longer first appointment with the practice nurse, numbing cream, and the hospital’s learning disability liaison nurse. If Danny can’t manage something even with help, we’ll look at whether he can make that decision, and if not, what is in his best interests, with you and his team. We’ll decide each step as we come to it.
model.why: Decision-specific capacity and best-interests process under the Mental Capacity Act 2005

model.text: Danny, if there’s a lot of blood, bad tummy pain, or you feel dizzy or very poorly, tell Maria straight away. Maria, that’s a same-day call to us, or 999 if he’s collapsing. I’ll keep track of the FIT result and the hospital appointment myself.
model.why: Specific safety-net and personal ownership of tracking

model.text: (Maria) “Thank you. That’s the first time someone’s said they’ll chase it.”
Danny, what will you tell the staff at home about today?
(Danny) “Poo test. Blood test. Maria come.”
Perfect. I’ll send an easy-read sheet today, and we’ll talk again when the results are back. Thank you both — Danny, you did really well.
model.why: Closes with accessible information and a defined review

social.t: Danny lives with a support team who notice changes before he reports them. Their observations of stools, eating and weight are key data — ask for them and plan with them.
Anxiety about appointments is a predictable barrier. Plan desensitisation, numbing cream, familiar people and quiet timing rather than repeating the same approach.

legal.t: Five principles: presume capacity, support decision-making, allow unwise decisions, act in best interests if capacity is lacking, choose the least restrictive option. Capacity is assessed per decision and per time; record the assessment and any best-interests decision.
Services must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Failing to adjust — so that a referral cannot be completed — can be unlawful as well as unsafe.
NHS England standard (DCB1605): identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs, including on referrals to hospital.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) requires you to treat each patient as an individual and not discriminate. LeDeR findings show avoidable deaths linked to delayed diagnosis in people with a learning disability.
Own the FIT result and the referral: a named person checks the result comes back and the appointment is attended.

community.t: Community learning disability team, hospital learning disability liaison nurse, and the annual learning disability health check (age 14 and over) with a health action plan.
Easy-read leaflets (for example Mencap and the NHS bowel cancer screening easy-read guides) and a hospital passport (made with his team if he has none) shared with the hospital.

redFlags: Rectal bleeding, change to looser stools and weight loss at 52 → FIT; refer on a suspected cancer pathway if at least 10 µg Hb/g (NICE NG12)
Rectal or anal mass, or unexplained anal ulceration on examination → refer without waiting for FIT
Heavy bleeding, melaena, dizziness or collapse → same-day assessment or 999
psychosocial: Establish his baseline with the support worker so new symptoms are recognised as new
Anxiety about appointments and fear of what the tests involve
Who supports him day to day, and who should be involved in decisions he cannot make
ice: Idea (Maria): something new is wrong and needs checking
Concern: it will be put down to nerves, or the tests will be too frightening to complete
Expectation: a way through the appointments that Danny can manage

playbook.diagnosis: Be honest without alarm: “Blood, looser stools and weight loss need proper checks in anyone of Danny’s age. I’m not going to put this down to nerves. The poo test and a camera test will tell us what’s going on.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Danny, sometimes the inside of the tummy gets a sore place that bleeds. The poo test helps the doctors know where to look, and the camera test lets them see inside and fix it.”

management.reflectIce: “Maria, you were worried this would be put down to nerves. It won’t. And because you told me how hard appointments are for him, I’m going to plan this so Danny can manage it.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around Danny: longer appointments, numbing cream, a familiar supporter, easy-read letters, the liaison nurse, and help with bowel preparation — agreed with him and his team.
sharedPlan: FIT at home with support; FBC, ferritin, U&E, CRP, TFTs, coeliac serology; face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE if he consents
Suspected cancer pathway referral if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g, or on a mass or anal ulceration, or if concern persists despite a low FIT
Capacity assessed for each decision; best-interests process with his team if he lacks capacity for a specific step
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, black stools, severe pain, dizziness or collapse → same day or 999
GP personally tracks the FIT result and referral; review to share results together

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on who you talk to and what you assume, not on colorectal knowledge. The patterns below are the common ways a correct plan still fails.

items.fail: Taking the whole history from Maria while Danny sits silently.
items.why: “Does not involve the patient” — the adjusted consultation is the core task. Talking over him scores poorly in Relating to Others.
items.fix: Greet Danny first, ask him short concrete questions, offer pointing or showing, and use Maria to add detail.

items.fail: Accepting ‘it might be his nerves’ and planning to watch and wait.
items.why: Diagnostic overshadowing. Rectal bleeding, looser stools and weight loss at 52 are a FIT and suspected cancer pathway picture under NICE NG12.
items.fix: Ask what is new against his baseline, then say plainly: “I take these symptoms seriously in anyone.”

items.fail: Direct suspected cancer pathway referral with no FIT, or FIT with no plan for a low result.
items.why: Current NICE NG12 and HTG690 practice is FIT-led: refer if at least 10 µg Hb/g; refer without FIT only for a rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration; a low FIT must not delay referral if concern persists.
items.fix: Offer FIT, examine face to face, and state the conditional plan for each result.

items.fail: “He has Down’s syndrome, so his support worker will consent.”
items.why: Mental Capacity Act 2005: capacity is presumed and decision-specific. A support worker cannot consent for an adult.
items.fix: Support his understanding, assess each decision, and use a documented best-interests process only if he lacks capacity for that decision.

items.fail: A standard referral letter with no adjustments, then no follow-up.
items.why: The investigation fails at bowel prep or the waiting room, and the cancer is found late. That is the health inequality this case is about.
items.fix: Write named adjustments into the referral, share the hospital passport, involve the liaison nurse, and track it personally.

items.fail: Jargon: “We’ll do a FIT and a suspected cancer referral (2WW) for a colonoscopy.”
items.why: Language not pitched to the patient. Danny cannot take part in decisions he cannot follow.
items.fix: “A poo test that looks for blood. Then a camera test at the hospital, with Maria there.” Check with teach-back.

SCA_MODELS.text: (Danny) “Red. In the toilet.” (Maria) “Sometimes it’s on the paper, sometimes it’s mixed in.”
Thank you, Danny, that really helps. Does your tummy hurt? Can you show me where?
SCA_MODELS.why: Asks about pain directly rather than through the carer

SCA_MODELS.text: (Danny shrugs.) “Don’t know.” (Maria) “He hasn’t told us about any pain.”
Maria, you know Danny well. How has his toileting changed, and when did you first notice? And has he lost weight on the scales, or is it clothes fitting differently?
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses the carer for collateral history on timing and weight

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “About two months. Looser, and more often. He’s gone off his food, and I think he’s lost a bit of weight, but we haven’t weighed him properly.”
That’s important. Is this different from how Danny usually is? I want to be sure we treat it as something new, not just ‘how he is’.
SCA_MODELS.why: Establishes a baseline — the active guard against diagnostic overshadowing

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “It’s definitely new. Honestly, I was worried someone would say it’s just his nerves.”
Any vomiting, very dark or black stools, feeling faint, or bleeding a lot at once?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for acute bleeding needing same-day care

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “No, nothing like that.”
Maria, you said you worried it might be put down to nerves. Can you tell me more about that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the carer’s cue about being dismissed

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “Danny gets very anxious about appointments. I’m worried the hospital tests will be too much for him, and then they just won’t happen.”
Thank you — that’s exactly what I need to plan for. Danny, how do you feel about doctors and hospitals?
SCA_MODELS.why: Brings Danny’s own feelings into the consultation

SCA_MODELS.text: (Danny) “Scared.”
That makes sense, Danny. Lots of people feel scared of doctors. We’ll make a plan so it’s less scary, and Maria can be with you. Is that okay?
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the fear in plain words and offers support

SCA_MODELS.text: (Danny nods.) “Maria come.”

Maria, let me be clear: blood from the bottom, looser stools and losing weight are things I take seriously in anyone of Danny’s age. His Down’s syndrome doesn’t change that — if anything, I want to be more careful, not less.
SCA_MODELS.why: States plainly that the symptoms are physical and warrant full assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: Danny, I’d like three things. One: a poo test you do at home — it looks for tiny bits of blood. Two: a blood test. Three: a check of your tummy, in person, with Maria there. Can you tell me back what the poo test is for?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains FIT, bloods and examination simply, then checks understanding

SCA_MODELS.text: (Danny) “Blood. In poo.”

Exactly right. Well done. Maria, the test result decides how fast the hospital sees him, and I’m expecting to refer him urgently to the bowel team for a camera test. The aim is to know within about four weeks. I’ll put on the referral that he needs a longer slot, a familiar person with him, easy-read letters, and help with the bowel preparation. Does he have a hospital passport? If not, the team could put one together.
SCA_MODELS.why: NICE NG12 FIT-led referral, with reasonable adjustments written into the referral

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “I’ll check with the team. What about his blood test — he finds that sort of thing really hard.”

I’ll book a longer first appointment with the practice nurse, numbing cream, and the hospital’s learning disability liaison nurse. If Danny can’t manage something even with help, we’ll look at whether he can make that decision, and if not, what is in his best interests, with you and his team. We’ll decide each step as we come to it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Decision-specific capacity and best-interests process under the Mental Capacity Act 2005

SCA_MODELS.text: Danny, if there’s a lot of blood, bad tummy pain, or you feel dizzy or very poorly, tell Maria straight away. Maria, that’s a same-day call to us, or 999 if he’s collapsing. I’ll keep track of the FIT result and the hospital appointment myself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net and personal ownership of tracking

SCA_MODELS.text: (Maria) “Thank you. That’s the first time someone’s said they’ll chase it.”
Danny, what will you tell the staff at home about today?
(Danny) “Poo test. Blood test. Maria come.”
Perfect. I’ll send an easy-read sheet today, and we’ll talk again when the results are back. Thank you both — Danny, you did really well.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with accessible information and a defined review

SCA_STEM.name: Danny Okafor
pmh: Moderate learning disability (on the practice learning disability register)
SCA_STEM.recent: Support team contacted the practice: about 2 months of rectal bleeding (bright red and sometimes mixed with stool), looser and more frequent stools, reduced appetite and possible weight loss. Attends by video with his long-standing support worker, Maria. Record notes that he becomes anxious at appointments.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation booked by his support team about bleeding from the back passage.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (2023, formerly DG56) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Code of Practice · Equality Act 2010 · NHS England Accessible Information Standard (DCB1605)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Rectal bleeding, looser stools and weight loss at 52 are a suspected colorectal cancer picture in anyone. Offer FIT, examine face to face, and refer on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT is 10 µg Hb/g or more — with the reasonable adjustments that let Danny actually get through it.

points.t: NICE HTG690 and NICE NG12: offer quantitative FIT to adults with a change in bowel habit, or aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss. Danny qualifies on more than one count. FIT at least 10 µg Hb/g → suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer.

points.h: When not to wait for FIT
points.t: A rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred on the examination finding without FIT. If FIT is below 10 µg Hb/g but strong clinical concern persists, NICE HTG690 says do not let the result delay referral.

Face-to-face abdominal examination and a DRE only with consent and at his pace. FBC and ferritin (iron-deficiency anaemia is itself a FIT indication), U&E, CRP, TFTs and coeliac serology (NICE NG20: offer testing for unexplained weight loss or persistent GI symptoms).

Do not put new physical symptoms down to the learning disability, Down’s syndrome or anxiety. LeDeR (Learning from lives and deaths) reviews repeatedly find delayed diagnosis of treatable illness in people with a learning disability.

Presume capacity; take all practicable steps to support it; assess for each decision (examination, FIT, colonoscopy) whether he can understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate. If he lacks capacity for a specific decision, decide in his best interests after consulting those who know him, and record how you reached it.

Equality Act 2010 duty: longer or first-of-day appointments, a quiet space, easy-read information, a familiar supporter, and flagging adjustments on the referral (Accessible Information Standard; Reasonable Adjustment flag where available). The NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims to confirm or rule out cancer within 28 days of referral.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Greeted Danny first; asked him directly, with pointing or showing as options; let Maria add, not replace.
Explored his usual toileting, eating and supported-living routine, the support team’s view, and the barrier of his anxiety about appointments.
Picked up Maria’s worry that it would be ‘put down to nerves’ and that the tests would be too much for him, and planned around both.
Idea: something new is wrong. Concern: dismissal and a frightening, uncompleted work-up. Expectation: help that he can actually manage. Danny’s own fear asked about.
Face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE with consent at his pace; FIT; FBC, ferritin, U&E, CRP, TFTs, coeliac serology.
Colorectal cancer, polyps, IBD, haemorrhoids or fissure, coeliac disease and thyroid disease — each tested, none assumed from the disability.
Screened for heavy bleeding, melaena, collapse; knows a rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration is referred without waiting for FIT.
Named a suspected colorectal cancer picture needing FIT and urgent investigation, stated without alarm.
FIT-led suspected cancer pathway referral (≥10 µg Hb/g) with reasonable adjustments written in; decision-specific capacity and best interests handled correctly.
Planned for anxiety about appointments and tests (numbing cream, familiar supporter, liaison nurse); flagged bowel prep support.
Named same-day and 999 symptoms; personal tracking of FIT and referral; easy-read information; booked review of results.

social.t: Danny lives with a support team who notice changes before he reports them. Their observations of stools, eating and weight are key data — ask for them and plan with them.
Anxiety about appointments is a predictable barrier. Plan desensitisation, numbing cream, familiar people and quiet timing rather than repeating the same approach.

legal.t: Five principles: presume capacity, support decision-making, allow unwise decisions, act in best interests if capacity is lacking, choose the least restrictive option. Capacity is assessed per decision and per time; record the assessment and any best-interests decision.
Services must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Failing to adjust — so that a referral cannot be completed — can be unlawful as well as unsafe.
NHS England standard (DCB1605): identify, record, flag, share and meet communication needs, including on referrals to hospital.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) requires you to treat each patient as an individual and not discriminate. LeDeR findings show avoidable deaths linked to delayed diagnosis in people with a learning disability.
Own the FIT result and the referral: a named person checks the result comes back and the appointment is attended.

community.t: Community learning disability team, hospital learning disability liaison nurse, and the annual learning disability health check (age 14 and over) with a health action plan.
Easy-read leaflets (for example Mencap and the NHS bowel cancer screening easy-read guides) and a hospital passport (made with his team if he has none) shared with the hospital.

redFlags: Rectal bleeding, change to looser stools and weight loss at 52 → FIT; refer on a suspected cancer pathway if at least 10 µg Hb/g (NICE NG12)
Rectal or anal mass, or unexplained anal ulceration on examination → refer without waiting for FIT
Heavy bleeding, melaena, dizziness or collapse → same-day assessment or 999
psychosocial: Establish his baseline with the support worker so new symptoms are recognised as new
Anxiety about appointments and fear of what the tests involve
Who supports him day to day, and who should be involved in decisions he cannot make
ice: Idea (Maria): something new is wrong and needs checking
Concern: it will be put down to nerves, or the tests will be too frightening to complete
Expectation: a way through the appointments that Danny can manage

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be honest without alarm: “Blood, looser stools and weight loss need proper checks in anyone of Danny’s age. I’m not going to put this down to nerves. The poo test and a camera test will tell us what’s going on.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Danny, sometimes the inside of the tummy gets a sore place that bleeds. The poo test helps the doctors know where to look, and the camera test lets them see inside and fix it.”

management.reflectIce: “Maria, you were worried this would be put down to nerves. It won’t. And because you told me how hard appointments are for him, I’m going to plan this so Danny can manage it.”
management.psychosocial: Build the plan around Danny: longer appointments, numbing cream, a familiar supporter, easy-read letters, the liaison nurse, and help with bowel preparation — agreed with him and his team.
sharedPlan: FIT at home with support; FBC, ferritin, U&E, CRP, TFTs, coeliac serology; face-to-face abdominal examination and DRE if he consents
Suspected cancer pathway referral if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g, or on a mass or anal ulceration, or if concern persists despite a low FIT
Capacity assessed for each decision; best-interests process with his team if he lacks capacity for a specific step
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, black stools, severe pain, dizziness or collapse → same day or 999
GP personally tracks the FIT result and referral; review to share results together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed on who you talk to and what you assume, not on colorectal knowledge. The patterns below are the common ways a correct plan still fails.

items.fail: Taking the whole history from Maria while Danny sits silently.
items.why: “Does not involve the patient” — the adjusted consultation is the core task. Talking over him scores poorly in Relating to Others.
items.fix: Greet Danny first, ask him short concrete questions, offer pointing or showing, and use Maria to add detail.

items.fail: Accepting ‘it might be his nerves’ and planning to watch and wait.
items.why: Diagnostic overshadowing. Rectal bleeding, looser stools and weight loss at 52 are a FIT and suspected cancer pathway picture under NICE NG12.
items.fix: Ask what is new against his baseline, then say plainly: “I take these symptoms seriously in anyone.”

items.fail: Direct suspected cancer pathway referral with no FIT, or FIT with no plan for a low result.
items.why: Current NICE NG12 and HTG690 practice is FIT-led: refer if at least 10 µg Hb/g; refer without FIT only for a rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration; a low FIT must not delay referral if concern persists.
items.fix: Offer FIT, examine face to face, and state the conditional plan for each result.

items.fail: “He has Down’s syndrome, so his support worker will consent.”
items.why: Mental Capacity Act 2005: capacity is presumed and decision-specific. A support worker cannot consent for an adult.
items.fix: Support his understanding, assess each decision, and use a documented best-interests process only if he lacks capacity for that decision.

items.fail: A standard referral letter with no adjustments, then no follow-up.
items.why: The investigation fails at bowel prep or the waiting room, and the cancer is found late. That is the health inequality this case is about.
items.fix: Write named adjustments into the referral, share the hospital passport, involve the liaison nurse, and track it personally.

items.fail: Jargon: “We’ll do a FIT and a suspected cancer referral (2WW) for a colonoscopy.”
items.why: Language not pitched to the patient. Danny cannot take part in decisions he cannot follow.
items.fix: “A poo test that looks for blood. Then a camera test at the hospital, with Maria there.” Check with teach-back.
